content: Adherence to the recommended guidelines can serve as a quality criterion or performance indicator in clinical practice. Clinicians must recognize that treatment choices should be tailored to each individual, taking into account their values and preferences. Decision aids may assist individuals in making choices that align with their personal values and preferences. Policy-making in this area requires extensive debate and the involvement of various stakeholders. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of managing conflicts of interest during the development process. Declarations of interest were obtained from all members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) and the External Review Group (ERG) before they assumed their roles. These declarations were disclosed at the beginning of GDG meetings, including subgroup meetings, and are summarized in accordance with WHO recommendations. Eleven members of the STI GDG declared interests, but all were deemed eligible for full participation as their conflicts were unrelated to the treatment of the infections or conditions under discussion. New treatment recommendations are provided for infections caused by Trichomonas vaginalis, Mycoplasma genitalium, and Candida albicans, whether symptomatic or asymptomatic. Recommendations also address bacterial vaginosis (BV) and anogenital warts caused by certain types of human papillomavirus (HPV). These guidelines apply to all adults and adolescents (aged 10–19 years), including pregnant and breastfeeding individuals (with some exceptions), as well as people living with HIV and key populations at higher risk of HIV due to specific behaviors, such as men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, prisoners, sex workers, and transgender individuals. Trichomonas vaginalis is a motile, flagellated protozoan that infects the vagina, urethra, and paraurethral glands in women, and the urethra and subpreputial sac in men. It is sexually transmitted, and global estimates suggest millions of new cases annually. The infection is often asymptomatic in at least 50% of women and up to 70–80% of men. In women, it can cause abnormal vaginal discharge (trichomoniasis), which is unlikely to resolve without treatment. The infection is associated with adverse reproductive health outcomes, including low birth weight, preterm delivery, and preterm premature rupture of membranes. It can also lead to pelvic inflammatory disease and an increased risk of HIV acquisition. There is evidence linking T. vaginalis to cervical carcinogenesis, particularly in women co-infected with HPV. In men, T. vaginalis can cause non-gonococcal urethritis, prostatitis, and reduced fertility. It has also been associated with increased HIV shedding in seminal fluid, potentially raising the risk of HIV transmission. Perinatal transmission of T. vaginalis is rare but can result in vaginal and respiratory infections in newborns. Non-sexual transmission is also rare but has been reported in cases involving contaminated washcloths, toilet seats, shared bathing water, and other items. Detection of T. vaginalis in young girls should prompt careful assessment to rule out sexual abuse. Clinical features of T. vaginalis infection in women include abnormal vaginal discharge, often described as yellow or greenish and frothy, along with vulval itching, erythema, and edema. On examination, a strawberry cervix (punctate hemorrhages on the cervix) may be observed, which is highly indicative of infection. In men, over 50% of infections are asymptomatic, but symptomatic cases may present with urethral discharge and dysuria. The incubation period for urethritis caused by T. vaginalis in men is estimated to be 3–9 days. Diagnosis of T. vaginalis can be achieved through wet mount microscopy, antigen detection assays, culture, and nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs). Wet mount microscopy is quick and inexpensive but requires immediate sample analysis to detect motile trichomonads. NAATs are the most sensitive diagnostic method and can identify infections in asymptomatic individuals, facilitating treatment to prevent transmission. Vaginal swabs are the preferred sample type for women, while urine and urethral swabs are used for men. Integrating T. vaginalis testing into existing NAAT-based programs for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis is recommended. Treatment for T. vaginalis infections includes metronidazole 400–500 mg orally twice daily for 7 days. For individuals with adherence concerns, a single 2 g dose of metronidazole or tinidazole (except during pregnancy) may be used. Sexual partners of infected individuals should also be treated to prevent reinfection. While T. vaginalis infection in men is often considered benign and self-limiting, it is important to assess and treat male partners of infected women, as many are also infected. Mycoplasma genitalium is a sexually transmitted bacterium with a flask-shaped morphology and the smallest known genome capable of self-replication. It lacks a cell wall, making it resistant to β-lactam antibiotics such as penicillins and cephalosporins. It is commonly found in the human urogenital tract and has been associated with non-gonococcal urethritis, epididymitis, and chronic prostatitis in men, as well as cervicitis, pelvic inflammatory disease, and bacterial vaginosis in women. Routine screening for M. genitalium is not recommended except in cases of recurrent symptomatic episodes. Diagnosis is best achieved through molecular techniques like PCR, ideally with macrolide resistance testing.
